claims.claim: Practically none of the ship's original timber survived, but its form remained
claims.quote: Although practically none of the original timber survived, the form of the ship was perfectly preserved.

claims.claim: Stains in the sand had replaced the timber
claims.quote: Stains in the sand had replaced the wood but had preserved many construction details.

claims.claim: Nearly every iron rivet still sat where it was driven
claims.quote: Nearly all of the iron planking rivets were in their original places.

claims.claim: The helmet photographed is held at the British Museum
claims.quote: The site is in the care of the National Trust; most of the objects found there are held by the British Museum.

claims.claim: Looters dug into the mound and missed the burial
claims.quote: when looters dug into the apparent centre during the sixteenth century, they missed the real centre

claims.claim: In medieval times the west end of the mound was dug away
claims.quote: In medieval times the westerly end of the mound was dug away and a boundary ditch was laid out.

claims.claim: Sixteenth-century diggers aimed at the apparent centre, not the real one
claims.quote: In the 16th century, a pit, dated by bottle shards left at the bottom, was dug into Mound 1, narrowly missing the burial.

claims.claim: The photograph shows Mound 1 at Sutton Hoo, taken in 2011
claims.quote:
Description: Rædwald's burial mound (Mound I), Sutton Hoo
Date: 2011-08-17

claims.claim: Basil Brown was a self-taught archaeologist
claims.quote: The site was first excavated by Basil Brown, a self-taught archaeologist, under the auspices of the landowner Edith Pretty.

claims.claim: Basil Brown was paid 30 shillings a week
claims.quote: In June 1938, Pretty took him to the site, offered him accommodation and a wage of 30 shillings a week, and suggested that he start digging at Mound 1.

claims.claim: Brown was told to stop digging but kept going, which may have saved the site from looters
claims.quote: Initially, Phillips and the British Museum instructed Brown to cease excavating until they could get their team assembled, but he continued working, something which may have saved the site from being looted by treasure hunters.

claims.claim: The photograph of Basil Brown dates from 1939
claims.quote:
FILE: basilbrown.jpg
Archive title: File:Basil Brown.jpg
Description: Basil Brown
Date: 1939

claims.claim: A treasure trove inquest ruled the finds were Edith Pretty's property as landowner
claims.quote: it was decided that since the treasure was buried without the intention to recover it, it was the property of Pretty as the landowner

claims.claim: Pretty gave the treasure to the nation
claims.quote: Pretty decided to bequeath the treasure as a gift to the nation, so that the meaning and excitement of her discovery could be shared by everyone.

claims.claim: Edith Pretty owned the land and paid for the dig
claims.quote: In June 1938, Pretty took him to the site, offered him accommodation and a wage of 30 shillings a week, and suggested that he start digging at Mound 1.

claims.claim: Her gift was at the time the largest made to the British Museum by a living donor
claims.quote: The ship-burial treasure was presented to the nation by the owner, Edith Pretty, and was at the time the largest gift made to the British Museum by a living donor.

claims.claim: No body was found; only a chemical stain
claims.quote: As a body was not found, there was early speculation that the ship-burial was a cenotaph rather than a grave.  The only sign of body being a chemical stain which could have had other origins

claims.claim: Soil analyses in 1967 found phosphate traces, suggesting a body had dissolved
claims.quote: Soil analyses conducted in 1967 found phosphate traces, supporting the view that a body had disappeared in the acidic soil.

claims.claim: Rædwald is the favourite candidate for the burial, though the evidence is disputed
claims.quote: Carver,  says Chadwick's identification was "repeatedly endorsed by other scholars for fifty years", and that Rædwald "is still the favourite candidate".

claims.claim: The photographed object is a sword-belt end ornament dated 625–630, photographed by Gary Todd, CC0
claims.quote: Archive title: File:Anglo-Saxon Sword Belt End Ornament from Sutton Hoo Burial, 625-630 AD.jpg

claims.claim: The ship-burial was discovered under Mound 1 in 1939
claims.quote: The ship-burial discovered under Mound 1 in 1939 contained one of the most magnificent archaeological finds in England

claims.claim: Sutton Hoo is near Woodbridge in Suffolk
claims.quote: Sutton Hoo is the site of two Anglo-Saxon cemeteries dating from the 6th to 7th centuries near Woodbridge, Suffolk, England.

claims.claim: The vessel was 27 metres long and 4.4 metres in the beam
claims.quote: It was possible to survey the original ship, which was found to be 27 metres (89 ft) long, pointed at either end with tall rising stem and stern posts and widening to 4.4 metres (14 ft) in the beam amidships

claims.claim: The hull was built clinker-fashion with nine planks a side
claims.quote: From the keel board, the hull was constructed clinker-fashion with nine planks on either side, fastened with rivets.

claims.claim: Twenty-six wooden ribs stiffened the ship
claims.quote: Twenty-six wooden ribs strengthened the form.

claims.claim: Oar-rests along the gunwales suggest room for forty rowers
claims.quote: In the fore and aft sections along the gunwales, there were oar-rests shaped like the Old English letter "thorn", indicating that there may have been positions for forty oarsmen.

claims.claim: The burial chamber held a helmet, sword, lyre and silver plate from the Eastern Roman Empire
claims.quote: The artefacts found in the ship's burial chamber included a suite of dress fittings in gold and gems, a ceremonial helmet, a shield, a sword, a lyre, and silver plate from the Eastern Roman Empire.

claims.claim: The great gold buckle contained a hidden chamber
claims.quote: The plate is hollow and has a hinged back, forming a secret chamber, possibly for a relic.

claims.claim: The purse held thirty-seven gold coins, each from a different Frankish mint
claims.quote: The purse contained thirty-seven gold shillings or tremisses, each originating from a different Frankish mint.

claims.claim: Rædwald of the East Angles has been the favourite candidate since 1940
claims.quote: Since 1940, when H.M. Chadwick first ventured that the ship-burial was probably the grave of Rædwald, Rædwald has been considered the most likely candidate.

claims.claim: A reference work calls the evidence for Rædwald "almost non-existent"
claims.quote: and by McClure and Collins, who note that the evidence for Rædwald is "almost non-existent"

claims.claim: In 2025 Helen Gittos argued the occupant was an elite local soldier who had fought for the Byzantine Empire
claims.quote: In 2025 Helen Gittos from Oxford University argued that the body was an elite local soldier who had fought for the Byzantine Empire, probably as a member of the cavalry troops known as the Foederati.
